title: AOEB: Benchmarking Agent-Oriented Multimodal Embeddings
one_liner: Test retrieval representations for agents on the tasks agents actually face, across code, tools, reasoning, memory, text, and images, so that evaluation matches practical agent use rather than generic search alone.
lead: Many agent systems depend on retrieval, yet the representations used for retrieval are still mostly judged on broad generic benchmarks. That creates a mismatch: a representation can look good on average search tasks and still be weak when an agent needs to recall a tool description, find a past memory, retrieve code, or connect text with an image. AOEB builds an agent-oriented benchmark to measure those practical differences directly, because agent retrieval is shaped by the tasks the agent must complete rather than by search quality in the abstract.

problem.h2: Why generic retrieval tests miss what agents need
paras: An agent does not retrieve documents for their own sake. It retrieves the next piece of information needed to act. That piece may be a code fragment, a tool description, an earlier memory, a reasoning hint, or a visual item tied to the current question. Generic retrieval tests often blur those cases together.

Because of that blur, a representation can rank well overall and still fail badly on one agent-critical use case. If an agent cannot retrieve the right tool usage note or the right past state, the whole task can fail. A benchmark for agent retrieval should therefore separate those capabilities instead of hiding them inside one average score.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Build a benchmark that splits agent retrieval into several practical task types and includes both text and image inputs so that retrieval representations are tested under agent-like workloads.

panels.viz_args: The next action depends on finding the right item
panels.caption: The needed item may be code, a tool note, a past memory, or a visual clue.

panels.viz_args: One broad score hides task-specific weaknesses
panels.caption: A high average score does not guarantee strength on the exact retrieval type the agent needs.

panels.viz_args: Code, tool, reasoning, memory, and multimodal retrieval

steps.text: Separate the major retrieval jobs agents rely on, such as code lookup, tool lookup, memory recall, and reasoning support.

steps.b: Build task sets for each capability
steps.text: Create evaluation tasks that reflect those retrieval jobs instead of relying on one undifferentiated search benchmark.

steps.b: Include both text and visual data
steps.text: Test each capability with multiple input forms because many agents work across screenshots, diagrams, and text instructions together.
Measure different representations on the same task families so that their strengths and weaknesses become visible.

steps.b: Report a capability profile, not one score alone
steps.text: Summarize how each representation behaves across tasks because the best choice depends on the agent workload.

paras: The paper changes what counts as a good retrieval benchmark for agents. Instead of one generic leaderboard, it offers a capability map that ties retrieval quality to concrete agent needs.
object.object: the evaluation target for retrieval representations used inside agent systems

hidden.name: which retrieval capability actually limits the agent on a given task
paras: A failed agent run may resemble a reasoning mistake when the real bottleneck was retrieval. The hidden part is which retrieval capability was missing: code lookup, tool lookup, memory recall, or cross-modal matching. A single average score does not reveal that bottleneck.

AOEB makes the bottleneck visible by separating retrieval types. Once the benchmark scores are broken down, a developer can see whether a representation is strong at recalling past context but weak at tool retrieval, or strong on text-only lookup but weak when images enter the task.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the agent-specific retrieval abilities that broad averages often hide.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is which kind of retrieval actually limits the agent on the task at hand.
The benchmark exposes distinct capability profiles by testing agent-centered retrieval tasks across both text and visual inputs.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: evaluate retrieval the way agents use it
paras: A representation used by an agent is only as helpful as its weakest important retrieval skill. If it cannot recover the right past memory or the right tool note, overall task performance can collapse even when its generic search score is high. Breaking evaluation into agent-relevant retrieval jobs reveals that mismatch.

The text-plus-visual design matters because many real agents work across screenshots, interfaces, diagrams, and written instructions. A text-only benchmark would miss those cases. AOEB therefore gives a more practical picture because it asks whether the retrieval representation can support the mixed workloads that modern agents actually face.

stages.s: A retrieval representation meant for agent use
Test it on several agent retrieval tasks
Test with both text and image inputs
A clearer choice of representation because task-specific strengths are no longer hidden

math.h2: Measure workload fit, not only average retrieval quality
math.words: A compact summary is to value one retrieval representation by averaging its performance across the agent retrieval capabilities that matter for the intended workload.
symbols: overall score of one retrieval representation for agent use
performance of the representation on one retrieval capability such as code, tools, memory, reasoning, or text-image matching
importance of that capability for the intended agent workload
add the weighted capabilities across the benchmark categories

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Model A is strong on code lookup and weak on memory recall.
Model B is the opposite: weaker on code lookup but stronger on memory recall and tool lookup.
If the target agent is a software assistant, the weights may favor code lookup.
If the target agent is a personal assistant, the weights may favor memory and tool lookup.
The benchmark is useful because it shows which model fits which workload.

math.note: The paper reports detailed benchmark results rather than one hand-designed formula, but this equation captures the central point that agent retrieval quality depends on workload composition.

charts.title: What a single broad average hides
charts.note: Broad generic tests hide important differences because they do not separate the retrieval jobs that agents actually perform.

charts.title: AOEB
charts.note: The benchmark reveals distinct strengths across models because it evaluates retrieval under agent-oriented task families instead of one undifferentiated average.

items.b: The benchmark can still miss future agent workloads.
items.html: Agent behavior changes quickly, so a task set that is practical today may become incomplete later because new tools and new interaction styles appear.
A task may need memory recall and reasoning support at once, so neat category splits can simplify reality more than developers would like.

items.b: A better benchmark does not by itself fix the model.
items.html: The benchmark reveals weak spots, but a weak representation still needs new training or design work because measurement alone does not improve retrieval.
The benchmark matters because it measures retrieval in the form agents actually consume it: as task-specific support for action.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark with four retrieval tracks: code lookup, tool documentation lookup, memory recall from past conversation state, and text-image matching from screenshots. Evaluate several retrieval models on the same tracks and report both the overall score and the per-track profile.

The demo should include at least one case where the best overall model is not the best model for a specific agent workload. That example matters because the paper's claim is that practical model choice changes when the retrieval job is broken down by agent need.
demo.metric_eq: profile_gap = best_overall_score - best_task_specific_score ; workload_fit = sum_i weight_i * capability_i
demo.closing: A good agent retrieval benchmark should tell you not only who wins overall, but also who is the right tool for the job.
